note: Every place this member models something no document settles, or where its two halves and the part itself could be read differently. Each entry names what stands behind the choice and what would change it. The list is short because the part's own boot program settles most of what this member adds.
authority: hardware.json holds the ladder. Rung one is empty, because Sony published nothing for this unit. Rung two has two things in it: the part's own boot program, which is where the console interface comes from, and checksums Shay Green took on a console, which settle what the boot program never touches. Below that are the records of the two members this unit is assembled from.

divergences.documentSays: Nothing. No Sony document for this unit is known.
divergences.referenceDoes: Implementations pick a ratio and step the two together, because a console emulator has to put them on one timeline somehow.
divergences.reasoning: The console and the audio unit run from separate crystals and neither divides the other, so any ratio is a property of one board rather than of the part. Publishing one would be publishing the single figure a caller most wants and having it be wrong everywhere, by an amount that drifts. This package publishes none and offers no elapsed time in console cycles.
divergences.wouldSettleIt: Nothing settles it, because there is nothing to settle: a measurement of both oscillators gives a ratio for that board. What would change this entry is a decision to model a whole console, which is not what this member is.

divergences.documentSays: Nothing from Sony. The SNESdev wiki states it outright: write-only registers read back as zero.
divergences.referenceDoes: Answers zero, which is now known to be what the part does.
divergences.reasoning: Five addresses are written and never read: the test register, the control register and the three timer dividers. This package answered with the memory underneath, on the grounds that inventing a value would be publishing a claim nobody measured. initial_regs.spc settled it by reading all sixteen registers in order and checksumming the result against a value taken on a console: of every arrangement of the five, exactly one reproduces it, and it is all five answering zero. The old behaviour was put back afterwards to watch the check fail, which it did, on sub-check 3 with d57e2579 against the wanted 9d4d2100.
divergences.wouldSettleIt: Settled by a measurement and by a document that agree. A Sony document would add a rung and would not change the answer.

divergences.referenceDoes: Places the sixteen registers as this package does.
divergences.reasoning: The boot program reaches 0xF1 through 0xF5, which settles the control register, the boot window bit and the first two ports from the part's own code. The other eleven addresses are not touched by those sixty four bytes, so their placement rests on agreement with implementations rather than on the artifact. This is now closed: the whole register file is checked at once rather than register by register, which is stronger than checking the ones the boot program happens to touch.
divergences.wouldSettleIt: Settled. initial_regs.spc reads every one of the sixteen and checksums them together against a value taken on a console.

divergences.referenceDoes: Clears everything, which is the one answer that is certainly wrong.
divergences.reasoning: What the processor holds coming out of reset is that member's question and its record answers it, including the one flag the boot program settles. What the sound generator holds is the other member's. This one adds memory, and memory holds whatever it held: nothing here is cleared at construction unless a caller asks for a fill, and building a unit resets neither half. The unit's reset() is the console's reset line and resets both.
divergences.wouldSettleIt: A capture of a real unit at power on. The two halves record it separately.

divergences.documentSays: Nothing. No Sony document for this unit is known.
divergences.referenceDoes: snes_spc, as snes9x 1.63 carries it, calls reset() from SPC_DSP::init, so its generator is reset before anything runs and nothing it holds at power on reaches memory.
divergences.reasoning: A unit is built with the generator and the processor scrambled, and the unit's reset() is the console's reset line, which resets both. A caller who runs a unit before that reset clocks the scrambled generator, and when its scrambled flag register leaves echo writes on it writes its echo buffer wherever its scrambled registers point. That is modelled rather than prevented. With the seed this package uses the flag register comes up as $25, whose bit 5 turns echo writes off, and a unit run for 64,000 cycles without a reset had its generator write nothing to memory.
divergences.wouldSettleIt: A logic capture of a real unit's memory bus from the rail coming up until the reset line is released, repeated across power cycles.

divergences.documentSays: Book I of Nintendo's development manual, page 3-5-2: at the time of reset, ST0 of the control register is 0, and the timer's counter and divider are indeterminate. Figure 3-4-3 gives the control register's reset value as --00-000. Nothing about memory, the ports or the other registers.
divergences.referenceDoes: Not compared: no implementation was read for what it does to these registers at a reset.
divergences.reasoning: reset() shows the boot window, stops all three timers, resets the generator and resets the processor, and leaves memory, the timers' dividers, stages and counters, the ports, the test register and the generator's address register holding what they held. The boot window has a source in the boot program: it never writes 0xF1 and the processor leaves reset through the vector at 0xFFFE, which only the boot program supplies. The timer starts have a source in the manual. Nothing settles the rest, and the family standard leaves what a reset does not define holding what it held.
divergences.wouldSettleIt: A capture of a real unit's registers and memory either side of a console reset, with the timers running and the ports written before it.

divergences.documentSays: Book I of Nintendo's development manual, Figure 3-5-1 and pages 3-5-1 and 3-5-2: one prescaler on a 2.048 MHz clock feeds timers 0 and 1 at 8 kHz and timer 2 at 64 kHz, switching a timer on clears its two counters, and the stage is cleared when its value corresponds to the divider.
divergences.referenceDoes: Shay Green's spc_smp.sfc random timer0, random timer0 enable and random timer2 checks, and its mem access times check, compare against values taken on a console.
divergences.reasoning: This model restarted a prescaler for each timer whenever one was switched on, and wrapped a divider lowered below the stage on the very next tick. Both disagree with what the manual draws and says, and the three random timer checks and the memory access check disagreed with the console. With one prescaler running from construction and never restarted, and the stage matched by equality so a lowered divider is reached after the stage wraps through 255, all eighteen verdicts the cartridge reaches agree, as recorded in cartridge.json.
divergences.wouldSettleIt: Settled by the document and by four checks taken on a console, run on 2026-10-19 against spc_smp.sfc, SHA-256 2ed302c5b989675d4ab6b40001fd5166ac4c6e0188a6b1b6df878e4608999c03, from https://gitlab.com/higan/snes-test-roms at commit 26e8aa91e0d3b90b901e7e693bc4a8244b391d7b.
